RuneScape CEO: We want to be bigger than World of Warcraft
We speak to Jagex boss Jon Bellamy about the company's complete focus on its three RuneScape games
Christopher Dring
Jul 21, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Jagex CEO Jon Bellamy on…
Taking on World of Warcraft
Old School’s surprising fanbase
The ‘pain’ of changing monetization
The console opportunity
Winning China
There’s a complaint on the RuneScape subreddit about a graphical bug.
There’s a fence that has impaled the edge of a barrel. It’s a pretty minor issue. Nevertheless, one person on that subreddit has made it their mission to get it fixed.
“He made a post every day saying: ‘Day 112 of waiting for this barrel to be fixed,’” says Jagex CEO Jon Bellamy.
“So, I sat with one of the lead designers and I asked, ‘Look, I’ve seen this Reddit post for the last 129 days. Are we going to do something?’ And he said, ‘What if we moved it further into the fence?’ I said, ‘That’s such a good idea.’ We then spent about a half a year moving it an inch further into the fence every day, and this guy responded every day with ‘day 400 of waiting for this stupid barrel thing to be over’.
“Now it is out of the fence with a hole where the fence was, leaking water forevermore. I think that playfulness is really who we are at our best. It makes this place turn over. It makes players happy.”
I enjoyed that story. Not only does it showcase the distinctive British whimsy that’s made RuneScape famous, but it also highlights how engaged Bellamy is with the franchise. He’s on the subreddits, he’s religiously playing the game (he was fishing in Old School RuneScape before our interview), and he’s at all the events (signing babies!).
And Jagex is RuneScape. There’s no other IP. No third-party publishing. It’s rebranded itself as Jagex: The RuneScape Company, and sold off its one non-RuneScape game, Scum, alongside its developer, Gamepires, to fellow UK studio Splash Damage.
“Never say never,” Bellamy says. “But I have no intention of going beyond RuneScape with this business.
“Our team size is less because we have fewer studios and products, but focus is through the roof. It’s really liberating to be able to do one thing better than anybody else in the world.”
“It’s really liberating to do one thing better than anybody else in the world”
That focus has manifested itself into three goals: Turn around its declining RuneScape MMO, invest heavily in the successful Old School RuneScape product, and fully release the survival game RuneScape: Dragonwilds.
We spoke to Bellamy about all this at Jagex’s offices in Cambridge, UK. And you can watch the full interview above (it’s a good one). Or check out the selected highlights below.

Jagex wants RuneScape to be the world’s No.1 MMO brand
RuneScape is the second biggest MMO brand globally, Jagex claims.
There’s bound to be debate over how you measure ‘biggest’, or indeed what is classed as an MMO, but regardless, Jagex sees itself as No.2, and it has its sights set on No.1: World of Waracraft.
“The dream is that we’re not the number two biggest MMO brand in the world,” says Bellamy. “We’re number one. There’s a big old gap between us and number one, but if we get it right, we know we can make headway. It’s lofty and ambitious, but if you’re going to set lofty and ambitious goals, why not swing for the top? So, that’s the number one goal.”
RuneScape monetization changes have stopped the decline (but it’s been painful)
Last year, Jagex changed how it monetizes RuneScape. It removed the unpopular (but lucrative) Treasure Hunter microtransaction, which gave players XP boosts, gold and gameplay-skipping items.
We spoke to Bellamy last year, who admitted that the company would likely take a financial hit by doing this, but change was necessary to get RuneScape back to growth.
Nine months later, has the company taken a financial hit? And have players come back?
“It has impacted revenue, not positively,” he says. “RuneScape revenue is down quite a large chunk. The reason why I took [this decision], the reason why we got the backing above me, is because I don’t think there was [any other] legitimate way to reset the standards for the game that would allow us to have a shot at coming back to growth. It has been painful, exactly as we thought it would be.”
Bellamy says that membership has stabilized for the first time in nearly four years, but user growth will require more than just changing monetization.
“Setting the table for growth is not the same as expecting growth to come as a result of setting the table. You need to put something on the table to bring people in. We’ve set the table, we’ve spent the last year not just removing that monetization layer, but overhauling so much of the clunkiness and the pain within the game.
“The guy who runs our RuneScape studio has been here for 13 years. He’s been a RuneScape player for 20. The person calling the shots on how to bring this thing back to life was a player in its golden age. He’s done a great job on getting the game into a healthy position. So less daily, less FOMO, less of the rubbish.
“I’ve been told very clearly not to give anything away, but on October 3 at RuneFest, we’ll be announcing our equivalent of putting a feast on the table, to really actively win people back, and that’ll be happening much sooner than many people expect.”
It may be retro, but half of Old School RuneScape players are new to the series
Old School RuneScape had a starring role in a new pop video
The core RuneScape game may be having a tough time, but the reverse is true of Old School RuneScape. “We broke just about every record we’ve ever had across every major metric in the last 12 months, and multiple times,” Bellamy says.
The retro version of RuneScape (it’s based on the 2007 version of the game) is growing, and Jagex will invest a further £200 million to turn it “into a stalwart product rather than a scrappy underdog.”
And it’s not just for older fans, either. In fact, half of Old School RuneScape’s active audience had never played a RuneScape game before.
“They’ve chosen to play the 2007 version as their first RuneScape experience,” Bellamy explains. “I think most people assume that this is something for the old-timers who’ve always been here. It’s not true. It stands alone.”
Why does he think that is?
“The easy answer is it’s great. But I think it’s a bit like some of the metal bands from the late ‘90s. You’re starting to see the Kylie Jenners of the world wearing Iron Maiden and Metallica T-shirts, and there’s a bunch of kids that I see that have no idea what Metallica is, but they love the font and think it’s a cool shirt. I have mixed feelings about that, but there is a bit of a resurgence, and we have that same feeling a bit with Old School.
“We have captured a portion of time that even those who weren’t there in their formative teenage years still long for. There’s a collective nostalgia for the simpler days before all the madness of social media.”
The game has even shown up in a new music video from artist Phoebe Bridgers.
“It’s like a real cross-cultural moment where in the middle of this like super poppy, very zeitgeisty music video, there’s a guy in a gas station playing Old School RuneScape,” Bellamy says. “It so well encapsulates what Old School is for so many people.”
Runescape: Dragonwilds is on 1.3 million sales and doing well in China
The third game in the RuneScape franchise is the survival game Dragonwilds, which launched into Early Access last year.
“We thought it was going to sell about 200,000 units in Early Access. We’re at about 1.3 million,” Bellamy says. “Since the beginning of this month, we’ve sold about another 100,000.”
That boost follows the game’s launch in Southeast Asia, including a version for Chinese players.
“RuneScape had zero presence in those countries. And part of that is because of what we make. [Our games have this] Monty Python-style, very British humor. It resonates really well in Finland. It resonates very well in Japan, as we’ve recently learned. It resonates very well in the Netherlands and the US. It’s very Western-centric. Or at least that’s what we’d assumed. And then we release a product in China for the first time, and in our first week following the release, 41% of sales have been to Chinese buyers. And since then, it’s evened out at about 15% to 20% a day.”
“So, maybe our long-held suspicions about cultural fit aren’t as true as we thought.”
Jagex thinks there’s 12 million former RuneScape players on Nintendo Switch
Dragonwilds will launch on PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo when it exits Early Access in September. It will be the first RuneScape game to ever launch on consoles.
“It’s a testing what we’ve always assumed to be not right for us,” he says. “Over the last 25 years, somebody somewhere looked at consoles, said it wasn’t going to be possible, probably not even worth it, and the upside isn’t that much. And that has just hung around in the walls of this place. This is our first legitimate ‘we’re actually going to do this thing’ moment. A new RuneScape product, tons of resource invested, tons of time invested, tons of heart. We’re going to bring it to new platforms where historically we’ve never been, and therefore it will be hard to get off the ground.
“We’ve done some numbers on this. We think there’s about six million of our historical players on each of the main platforms, so Xbox and PlayStation, and then about twice that on Switch. So, when we’ve been speaking with the platforms, I’ve been saying, ‘Look, you don’t need to create an audience for us. We have one. They’re there. Let’s bring them a game.’”
‘It’s not worth worrying about rising console prices and GTA 6’
Jagex faces a few challenges with Dragonwilds. It’s coming to consoles at a time when that sector is facing severe headwinds due to rising prices.
It also launches in a hyper congested September as publishers seek to avoid the launch of GTA 6 in November.
“September is congested, and yes, we’ll have to fight for our place,” Bellamy says. “But it is genuinely very good, and secondarily, we have this unique advantage of 300 million RuneScape players that we can really lean in on. That helps to de-risk a bit. But you’d be foolish to say that it isn’t harder today than it was six months ago.”
He continues: “It’s a control the controllables thing. I speak with my Board and my team and say, ‘Look, some of our expectations might need to shift a bit because GTA is launching in November. Everybody else is launching in September. Console prices are going through the roof. There’s a bunch of things changing around us that we can’t control.’
“Our job is to come to the places where players are, do our very best interpretation of giving them what they want, and carry on. The rest of it that is outside of our control isn’t really worth worrying about.”
Thank you for reading! We’ll be back Thursday with a special edition of The Game Business featuring Amazon. You won’t want to miss it.

There’s a complaint on the RuneScape subreddit about a graphical bug.

There’s a fence that has impaled the edge of a barrel. It’s a pretty minor issue. Nevertheless, one person on that subreddit has made it their mission to get it fixed.

“He made a post every day saying: ‘Day 112 of waiting for this barrel to be fixed,’” says Jagex CEO Jon Bellamy.

“So, I sat with one of the lead designers and I asked, ‘Look, I’ve seen this Reddit post for the last 129 days. Are we going to do something?’ And he said, ‘What if we moved it further into the fence?’ I said, ‘That’s such a good idea.’ We then spent about a half a year moving it an inch further into the fence every day, and this guy responded every day with ‘day 400 of waiting for this stupid barrel thing to be over’.

“Now it is out of the fence with a hole where the fence was, leaking water forevermore. I think that playfulness is really who we are at our best. It makes this place turn over. It makes players happy.”

I enjoyed that story. Not only does it showcase the distinctive British whimsy that’s made RuneScape famous, but it also highlights how engaged Bellamy is with the franchise. He’s on the subreddits, he’s religiously playing the game (he was fishing in Old School RuneScape before our interview), and he’s at all the events (signing babies!).

And Jagex is RuneScape. There’s no other IP. No third-party publishing. It’s rebranded itself as Jagex: The RuneScape Company, and sold off its one non-RuneScape game, Scum, alongside its developer, Gamepires, to fellow UK studio Splash Damage.

“Never say never,” Bellamy says. “But I have no intention of going beyond RuneScape with this business.

“Our team size is less because we have fewer studios and products, but focus is through the roof. It’s really liberating to be able to do one thing better than anybody else in the world.”

“It’s really liberating to do one thing better than anybody else in the world”

That focus has manifested itself into three goals: Turn around its declining RuneScape MMO, invest heavily in the successful Old School RuneScape product, and fully release the survival game RuneScape: Dragonwilds.

Whether planning your next launch or looking to grow your live service through creators, make sure to grab a chat with the Wehype team. Get in touch at partnerships@wehype.com or meet us at Gamescom.

Jagex wants RuneScape to be the world’s No.1 MMO brand

RuneScape is the second biggest MMO brand globally, Jagex claims.

There’s bound to be debate over how you measure ‘biggest’, or indeed what is classed as an MMO, but regardless, Jagex sees itself as No.2, and it has its sights set on No.1: World of Waracraft.

“The dream is that we’re not the number two biggest MMO brand in the world,” says Bellamy. “We’re number one. There’s a big old gap between us and number one, but if we get it right, we know we can make headway. It’s lofty and ambitious, but if you’re going to set lofty and ambitious goals, why not swing for the top? So, that’s the number one goal.”

RuneScape monetization changes have stopped the decline (but it’s been painful)

Last year, Jagex changed how it monetizes RuneScape. It removed the unpopular (but lucrative) Treasure Hunter microtransaction, which gave players XP boosts, gold and gameplay-skipping items.

We spoke to Bellamy last year, who admitted that the company would likely take a financial hit by doing this, but change was necessary to get RuneScape back to growth.

Nine months later, has the company taken a financial hit? And have players come back?

“It has impacted revenue, not positively,” he says. “RuneScape revenue is down quite a large chunk. The reason why I took [this decision], the reason why we got the backing above me, is because I don’t think there was [any other] legitimate way to reset the standards for the game that would allow us to have a shot at coming back to growth. It has been painful, exactly as we thought it would be.”

Bellamy says that membership has stabilized for the first time in nearly four years, but user growth will require more than just changing monetization.

“Setting the table for growth is not the same as expecting growth to come as a result of setting the table. You need to put something on the table to bring people in. We’ve set the table, we’ve spent the last year not just removing that monetization layer, but overhauling so much of the clunkiness and the pain within the game.

“The guy who runs our RuneScape studio has been here for 13 years. He’s been a RuneScape player for 20. The person calling the shots on how to bring this thing back to life was a player in its golden age. He’s done a great job on getting the game into a healthy position. So less daily, less FOMO, less of the rubbish.

“I’ve been told very clearly not to give anything away, but on October 3 at RuneFest, we’ll be announcing our equivalent of putting a feast on the table, to really actively win people back, and that’ll be happening much sooner than many people expect.”

It may be retro, but half of Old School RuneScape players are new to the series

The core RuneScape game may be having a tough time, but the reverse is true of Old School RuneScape. “We broke just about every record we’ve ever had across every major metric in the last 12 months, and multiple times,” Bellamy says.

The retro version of RuneScape (it’s based on the 2007 version of the game) is growing, and Jagex will invest a further £200 million to turn it “into a stalwart product rather than a scrappy underdog.”

And it’s not just for older fans, either. In fact, half of Old School RuneScape’s active audience had never played a RuneScape game before.

“They’ve chosen to play the 2007 version as their first RuneScape experience,” Bellamy explains. “I think most people assume that this is something for the old-timers who’ve always been here. It’s not true. It stands alone.”

Why does he think that is?

“The easy answer is it’s great. But I think it’s a bit like some of the metal bands from the late ‘90s. You’re starting to see the Kylie Jenners of the world wearing Iron Maiden and Metallica T-shirts, and there’s a bunch of kids that I see that have no idea what Metallica is, but they love the font and think it’s a cool shirt. I have mixed feelings about that, but there is a bit of a resurgence, and we have that same feeling a bit with Old School.

“We have captured a portion of time that even those who weren’t there in their formative teenage years still long for. There’s a collective nostalgia for the simpler days before all the madness of social media.”

The game has even shown up in a new music video from artist Phoebe Bridgers.

“It’s like a real cross-cultural moment where in the middle of this like super poppy, very zeitgeisty music video, there’s a guy in a gas station playing Old School RuneScape,” Bellamy says. “It so well encapsulates what Old School is for so many people.”

Runescape: Dragonwilds is on 1.3 million sales and doing well in China

The third game in the RuneScape franchise is the survival game Dragonwilds, which launched into Early Access last year.

“We thought it was going to sell about 200,000 units in Early Access. We’re at about 1.3 million,” Bellamy says. “Since the beginning of this month, we’ve sold about another 100,000.”

That boost follows the game’s launch in Southeast Asia, including a version for Chinese players.

“RuneScape had zero presence in those countries. And part of that is because of what we make. [Our games have this] Monty Python-style, very British humor. It resonates really well in Finland. It resonates very well in Japan, as we’ve recently learned. It resonates very well in the Netherlands and the US. It’s very Western-centric. Or at least that’s what we’d assumed. And then we release a product in China for the first time, and in our first week following the release, 41% of sales have been to Chinese buyers. And since then, it’s evened out at about 15% to 20% a day.”

“So, maybe our long-held suspicions about cultural fit aren’t as true as we thought.”

Jagex thinks there’s 12 million former RuneScape players on Nintendo Switch

Dragonwilds will launch on PlayStation, Xbox and Nintendo when it exits Early Access in September. It will be the first RuneScape game to ever launch on consoles.

“It’s a testing what we’ve always assumed to be not right for us,” he says. “Over the last 25 years, somebody somewhere looked at consoles, said it wasn’t going to be possible, probably not even worth it, and the upside isn’t that much. And that has just hung around in the walls of this place. This is our first legitimate ‘we’re actually going to do this thing’ moment. A new RuneScape product, tons of resource invested, tons of time invested, tons of heart. We’re going to bring it to new platforms where historically we’ve never been, and therefore it will be hard to get off the ground.

“We’ve done some numbers on this. We think there’s about six million of our historical players on each of the main platforms, so Xbox and PlayStation, and then about twice that on Switch. So, when we’ve been speaking with the platforms, I’ve been saying, ‘Look, you don’t need to create an audience for us. We have one. They’re there. Let’s bring them a game.’”

‘It’s not worth worrying about rising console prices and GTA 6’

Jagex faces a few challenges with Dragonwilds. It’s coming to consoles at a time when that sector is facing severe headwinds due to rising prices.

It also launches in a hyper congested September as publishers seek to avoid the launch of GTA 6 in November.

“September is congested, and yes, we’ll have to fight for our place,” Bellamy says. “But it is genuinely very good, and secondarily, we have this unique advantage of 300 million RuneScape players that we can really lean in on. That helps to de-risk a bit. But you’d be foolish to say that it isn’t harder today than it was six months ago.”

He continues: “It’s a control the controllables thing. I speak with my Board and my team and say, ‘Look, some of our expectations might need to shift a bit because GTA is launching in November. Everybody else is launching in September. Console prices are going through the roof. There’s a bunch of things changing around us that we can’t control.’

“Our job is to come to the places where players are, do our very best interpretation of giving them what they want, and carry on. The rest of it that is outside of our control isn’t really worth worrying about.”

title: 2026年AI应用市场洞察报告：竞争、商业与数字经济新格局
author: Sensor Tower
text:
这场始于 2023 年、由聊天机器人引发的变革，如今已演变为一场更广泛的生态系统转型。从 AI 助手、AI 赋能的购物体验，到 AI 概念在广告营销和非 AI 原生应用中的快速普及，AI正持续重塑产品、商业与用户体验。
纵观整个移动与网络生态，三大趋势正在定义2026 年的 AI 发展格局：
竞争格局升温，ChatGPT迎来更多挑战
AI 智能体正在改变消费者购物方式
AI 成为用户发现内容与广告触达的新入口
Sensor Tower 的《2026年AI应用市场洞察报告》 对上述及更多核心议题展开了深度剖析，全面覆盖了跨设备和跨垂直行业的最新趋势。
竞争格局升温，ChatGPT迎来更多挑战
ChatGPT 持续引领AI助手市场。在 2026 年 5 月，它成为了全球移动应用历史上最快达到 10 亿月活跃用户（MAU）的 App，而实现这一里程碑仅用了三年时间，速度超越了 TikTok、YouTube 和 Instagram。
尽管新竞品层出不穷，但该市场依然表现出高度集中的态势。2026 年第一季度，ChatGPT、Google Gemini 和 DeepSeek 的使用时长合占据 AI 助手类应用总时长的近 90%，显示少数头部平台仍占据主导地位。
然而，在这个高度集中的市场边缘，竞争已经开始加剧。由于 Google Gemini 和 Claude 在全球几个核心市场持续发力，ChatGPT 的真实受众（用于衡量跨移动应用端和网站端的去重独立用户规模）份额在 2026 年 3 月首次跌破了 50%。得益于强大的 Android 系统原生集成以及在谷歌各项服务中更广泛的生态分发，Google Gemini 稳步扩大了其市场版图，尤其是在欧洲、美国、日本和韩国。
Claude 则成为了 2026 年增长最快的黑马挑战者。2026年5月，其真实受众规模实现了 452% 的同比爆发式增长，在全美市场的份额也从 4.4% 攀升至近 14%。在美国市场，OpenAI 与美国战争部（Department of War）达成协议后，ChatGPT 的卸载量出现明显增长，并于3月9日至15日当周达到峰值，约为该应用平均水平的2倍。。由于 Anthropic 明确拒绝了与五角大楼的合作，许多卸载 ChatGPT 的用户似乎流向了 Claude。在 3 月 1 日至 5 日期间，Claude 的单日下载量曾一度超越 ChatGPT。虽然自 3 月 6 日以来ChatGPT在下载量日榜重新保持领先，但两者的差距已较 3 月前显著收窄。
数据表明，虽然 ChatGPT 依然是该品类中无可争议的领头羊，但由于 Gemini 具备结构性的渠道触达优势，加之 Claude 在专业人士和高意向用户群体中的快速渗透，市场正逐渐从单寡头垄断走向更多元的多强竞争格局。
AI 智能体正在改变消费者购物方式
AI 助手正在越来越多地影响消费者在网上发现和评估商品的方式，尤其是在高客单价、重度依赖调研对比的品类中（如电子数码、家居用品和时尚服饰）。从 2024 年第四季度到 2026 年第一季度，由生成式 AI 导流至购物网站的引荐流量在所有主流零售品类中均实现了增长。其中，电脑与消费电子品类领跑这一转变，生成式 AI 贡献的流量份额飙升了近四倍；同时，家居园艺和运动户外品类在总访问量中的占比也均突破了 0.35%。
不过，不同零售平台对AI技术的采用程度存在明显差异。诸如沃尔玛（Walmart）和塔吉特（Target）等深度集成 AI 助手的零售巨头，其获得生成式 AI 引荐流量的份额已攀升至 1.5% 以上。相比之下，亚马逊（Amazon）由于对爬虫访问采取了限制措施且整体生态相对封闭，该份额目前依然处于较低水平。
与此同时，各电商平台自身内置的早期AI购物助手，例如亚马逊的 Rufus 和沃尔玛的 Sparky，也在重塑用户的站内行为。数据显示，使用 Rufus 的用户，其购买转化率几乎是未使用用户的两倍。而 Sparky 的采用率在快速增长的同时，也显著拉长了用户的站内停留时长，并有效提升了客单价（订单金额）。
这表明，AI的价值不仅体现在引流，更体现在提升零售平台站内的转化效率与用户参与度。
AI 成为用户发现内容与广告触达的新入口
随着AI应用不断普及，AI正在成为继搜索和社交之后，数字生态中的新型内容发现入口。ChatGPT 在 2026 年年初开始测试广告投放，截至 5 月，其广告展示量较 3 月份大涨了 7 倍以上。虽然目前的整体渗透率仍处于早期低位，但 AI 平台正在迅速演变为广告主不可忽视的全新效果营销与用户触达渠道。
早期的广告主主要集中在购物、软件、旅游以及金融服务领域，这高度契合了 AI 协助用户进行复杂决策的天然优势。然而，相比于传统的社交媒体平台，AI 平台对医疗健康、博彩等敏感品类采取了更为严格的限制，从而构建起了一个更加精细合规的广告生态圈。
与此同时，AI 品牌自身也成为了市场的重要广告主。2026 年第一季度，美国市场在生成式 AI 相关广告上的投入同比激增超过 3 倍。随着用户获取的竞争全面白热化，OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的广告支出均实现了 800% 以上的同比飙升。
放眼更广泛的互联网大盘，借势 AI 概念的营销手段也已走向主流。目前已有超过 20 万款应用在商店描述中提及了 AI，而在 2026 年第一季度，全球包含 AI 相关关键词的广告素材投入达到13亿美元。
放眼全局
纵观 AI 助手、商业零售与广告营销三大领域，一个清晰的发展规律正逐渐显现：
AI 不再是一个单独的应用品类，而是正在演变为贯穿整个互联网的行为习惯与商业底层架，深刻重塑用户体验、商业模式和数字生态。
在 AI 助手赛道，市场正从一家独大走向多强竞争
在商业零售赛道，AI 正在重塑消费者的内容发现与购买转化路径
在广告营销赛道，AI 已经同时成为了投放媒介与核心卖点本身
在移动应用生态中，AI 正在从一项标新立异的独立产品转变为默认的标配功能
这些转变共同表明， 2026 年是 AI 跨越早期尝鲜阶段、全面结构性融入数字经济的成熟之年。
更多核心洞察
欢迎阅读 Sensor Tower《 2026年AI应用市场洞察报告 》，报告精彩看点包括：
生成式AI市场格局： 2026 年上半年全球生成式 AI 应用的总使用时长预计将达到 360 亿小时，较 2025 年上半年的 172 亿小时实现翻倍以上增长。
AI 消费者行为特征： ChatGPT 的人均每月使用时长已达到约 215 分钟。与此同时，Gemini（由 14 分钟狂揽至 100 分钟）和 Claude（由 40 分钟飙升至 120 分钟）的用户使用粘性也迎来了爆发式攀升。
生成式 AI 营销趋势： 随着获客争夺战进入白热化，2026 年第一季度美国生成式 AI 广告支出同比大涨超过 3 倍，其中 OpenAI 同比大涨超过 800%，Anthropic 同比大涨 1184%。
AI 跨行业落地渗透： 产品信息包含 AI 相关关键词的应用在 2026 年上半年有望斩获近 100 亿次下载，AI 应用正在向健康与保健、金融、教育和工具等多个领域扩展。
各行业 AI 广告营销趋势 ：2026 年第一季度主打 AI 概念的数字广告总支出达到 13 亿美元，展示量达 1670 亿次，其中健康与保健品类以 165% 的同比增速领跑大盘。

AI 助手正在越来越多地影响消费者在网上发现和评估商品的方式，尤其是在高客单价、重度依赖调研对比的品类中（如电子数码、家居用品和时尚服饰）。从 2024 年第四季度到 2026 年第一季度，由生成式 AI 导流至购物网站的引荐流量在所有主流零售品类中均实现了增长。其中，电脑与消费电子品类领跑这一转变，生成式 AI 贡献的流量份额飙升了近四倍；同时，家居园艺和运动户外品类在总访问量中的占比也均突破了 0.35%。

不过，不同零售平台对AI技术的采用程度存在明显差异。诸如沃尔玛（Walmart）和塔吉特（Target）等深度集成 AI 助手的零售巨头，其获得生成式 AI 引荐流量的份额已攀升至 1.5% 以上。相比之下，亚马逊（Amazon）由于对爬虫访问采取了限制措施且整体生态相对封闭，该份额目前依然处于较低水平。

与此同时，各电商平台自身内置的早期AI购物助手，例如亚马逊的 Rufus 和沃尔玛的 Sparky，也在重塑用户的站内行为。数据显示，使用 Rufus 的用户，其购买转化率几乎是未使用用户的两倍。而 Sparky 的采用率在快速增长的同时，也显著拉长了用户的站内停留时长，并有效提升了客单价（订单金额）。

这表明，AI的价值不仅体现在引流，更体现在提升零售平台站内的转化效率与用户参与度。

AI 成为用户发现内容与广告触达的新入口

随着AI应用不断普及，AI正在成为继搜索和社交之后，数字生态中的新型内容发现入口。ChatGPT 在 2026 年年初开始测试广告投放，截至 5 月，其广告展示量较 3 月份大涨了 7 倍以上。虽然目前的整体渗透率仍处于早期低位，但 AI 平台正在迅速演变为广告主不可忽视的全新效果营销与用户触达渠道。

早期的广告主主要集中在购物、软件、旅游以及金融服务领域，这高度契合了 AI 协助用户进行复杂决策的天然优势。然而，相比于传统的社交媒体平台，AI 平台对医疗健康、博彩等敏感品类采取了更为严格的限制，从而构建起了一个更加精细合规的广告生态圈。

与此同时，AI 品牌自身也成为了市场的重要广告主。2026 年第一季度，美国市场在生成式 AI 相关广告上的投入同比激增超过 3 倍。随着用户获取的竞争全面白热化，OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的广告支出均实现了 800% 以上的同比飙升。

放眼更广泛的互联网大盘，借势 AI 概念的营销手段也已走向主流。目前已有超过 20 万款应用在商店描述中提及了 AI，而在 2026 年第一季度，全球包含 AI 相关关键词的广告素材投入达到13亿美元。

放眼全局

纵观 AI 助手、商业零售与广告营销三大领域，一个清晰的发展规律正逐渐显现：

AI 不再是一个单独的应用品类，而是正在演变为贯穿整个互联网的行为习惯与商业底层架，深刻重塑用户体验、商业模式和数字生态。

  • 在 AI 助手赛道，市场正从一家独大走向多强竞争

  • 在商业零售赛道，AI 正在重塑消费者的内容发现与购买转化路径

  • 在广告营销赛道，AI 已经同时成为了投放媒介与核心卖点本身

  • 在移动应用生态中，AI 正在从一项标新立异的独立产品转变为默认的标配功能

这些转变共同表明， 2026 年是 AI 跨越早期尝鲜阶段、全面结构性融入数字经济的成熟之年。
